hero.name: Hero (Heron) of Alexandria
hero.role: Alexandrian geometer, mechanician, and optical physicist
hero.summary: Author of the Metrica, Dioptra, Mechanica, Pneumatica, Automata, Catoptrica, and Definitiones; dated securely via the lunar eclipse of 13 March 62 CE recorded in Dioptra Ch. 35. Unified Euclidean synthetic demonstration with Archimedean exhaustion and Babylonian-Egyptian numerical calculation.
hero.hero_loci: Metrica I–III passim; Dioptra Chs. 1–38; Catoptrica Prop. 4 (Schmidt pp. 324–329, 368–372); Definitiones §§1–138

archimedes.name: Archimedes of Syracuse
archimedes.summary: Hero's supreme mathematical authority throughout Books I and II of the Metrica; Hero cites Measurement of a Circle, On the Sphere and Cylinder, Quadrature of the Parabola, On Conoids and Spheroids, the lost Plinthides and Cylinders, and—uniquely before the 1906 Archimedes Palimpsest discovery—the Mechanical Method (Ἐφοδικόν). Arabic witnesses (al-Bīrūnī) also credit Archimedes with discovering the triangle area theorem proved in Metrica I.8.
archimedes.hero_loci: Metrica I.26, I.31–32, I.35, I.37–39; II.11–12, II.14–15 (Method), II.20 (hydrostatic crown/bath displacement)

euclid.name: Euclid of Alexandria
euclid.role: Author of the Elements, Data, On Divisions of Figures, and Optics
euclid.summary: Provides the deductive backbone of Hero's geometric analyses ('given in magnitude and form' via the Data, angle bisectors and cyclic quadrilaterals in Books III–IV, golden-section pentagon ratios in Book XIII, and area/solid divisions extending Euclid's lost On Divisions of Figures in Metrica Book III).
euclid.hero_loci: Metrica I.5–8, I.18, I.23, II.16–19, III.1–19; Definitiones passim

eudoxus.name: Eudoxus of Cnidus
eudoxus.role: Geometer and astronomer; discoverer of the cone/pyramid third-volume theorem
eudoxus.summary: Explicitly credited in Hero's Preface to Metrica Book II (together with Archimedes) as demonstrating before Archimedes that every cylinder is triple the cone on the same base and equal height, and every prism triple the pyramid.

dionysodorus.name: Dionysodorus of Caunos (or Melos)
dionysodorus.role: Hellenistic geometer; author of On the Torus (Περὶ τῆς σπείρας)
dionysodorus.summary: Hellenistic geometer whose lost treatise On the Torus (Περὶ τῆς σπείρας) is preserved solely through Hero's citation in Metrica II.13, establishing that the volume of a torus equals a cylinder on the centroid radius scaled by the ratio of the generating circle to half its meridian rectangle (V = 2π²Rr²).

plato.name: Plato
plato.role: Athenian philosopher; founder of the Academy
plato.summary: Named by Hero in Metrica II.15–19 as eponym of the Five Platonic Solids (cube, pyramid/tetrahedron, octahedron, icosahedron, dodecahedron) from the Timaeus, and echoed in Metrica III's Prooemium on proportional distributive justice (Laws VI 757b–c).
plato.hero_loci: Metrica II.15 (Schöne p. 132), III Preface (Schöne p. 140)

theaetetus.name: Theaetetus of Athens
theaetetus.role: Geometer of the Academy; classifier of irrationals and the five regular polyhedra
theaetetus.summary: Architect of the theory of quadratic irrationals (Elements X) and exact edge-to-circumradius constructions of the five regular solids (Elements XIII), which Hero translates into explicit edge-to-volume algorithms in Metrica II.16–19.

hipparchus.name: Hipparchus of Nicaea
hipparchus.role: Astronomer and founder of Greek chord trigonometry
hipparchus.summary: Pioneer of the treatise On Chords in a Circle (Περὶ τῶν ἐν κύκλῳ εὐθειῶν), the chord-table tradition invoked by Hero in Metrica I.22 and I.24 to compute the regular enneagon (9-gon) and hendecagon (11-gon).
hipparchus.hero_loci: Metrica I.22, I.24 (Schöne pp. 58–62); Dioptra Ch. 35

posidonius.name: Posidonius of Apamea
posidonius.role: Stoic philosopher, geographer, and mathematical foundationalist
posidonius.summary: Source for several kinematic and physical-conceptual supplements in Hero's Definitiones and Proclus's Commentary on Book I, defending Euclidean postulates and classifying quadrilaterals and parallels.

ptolemy.name: Claudius Ptolemy
ptolemy.role: Alexandrian astronomer, geometer, and optical theorist
ptolemy.summary: Paired with Hero by Olympiodorus as co-witness of the shortest-path reflection demonstration in Optics and Catoptrica, and successor to the chord-table tradition cited in Metrica I.22–24.

pappus.name: Pappus of Alexandria
pappus.role: Alexandrian geometer; author of the Synagoge (Collection)
pappus.summary: Preserves extensive testimony to Hero's Mechanics in Synagoge Book VIII and generalizes the torus centroid principle anticipated by Hero's 'unrolled cylinder' proof in Metrica II.13 into the Pappus-Guldin Centroid Theorem (Synagoge VII.42).

proclus.name: Proclus Diadochus
proclus.role: Neoplatonic philosopher; author of Commentary on Euclid's Elements Book I
proclus.summary: Repeatedly cites 'Heron the Mechanician' (Ἥρων ὁ μηχανικός) in his Commentary on Euclid Book I—recording Hero's proofs without reductio ad absurdum, his kinematic constructs, and his Economy of Postulates reducing Euclid's postulates to three.

olympiodorus.name: Olympiodorus the Younger
olympiodorus.summary: In his Commentary on Aristotle's Meteorology III.2, Olympiodorus preserves verbatim the original Greek text of Hero's variational shortest-path proof of the Law of Reflection from Hero's Catoptrica.

eutocius.name: Eutocius of Ascalon
eutocius.summary: Attests explicitly in his commentary on Archimedes' Measurement of a Circle that Hero explained the extraction of approximate square roots of non-square numbers in his Metrica.

al-biruni.name: Abū Rayḥān al-Bīrūnī
al-biruni.role: Mathematician, astronomer, and historian of science
al-biruni.summary: In his Book on the Finding of Chords in the Circle, al-Bīrūnī preserves the medieval Islamic geometric tradition attributing the triangle area rule Δ = √(s(s−a)(s−b)(s−c)) originally to Archimedes, whose earliest surviving Greek proof is Hero's Metrica I.8.

moerbeke.name: William of Moerbeke
moerbeke.role: Dominican translator of Greek mathematical and philosophical manuscripts
moerbeke.summary: Translated Hero's Catoptrica (under the title De speculis, long attributed to Ptolemy) and Archimedes' treatises into Latin at Viterbo in 1269, preserving the full proposition sequence of the Catoptrica alongside Olympiodorus's Greek fragment.

hultsch.name: Friedrich Otto Hultsch
hultsch.role: Classical philologist and historian of Greek metrology and mathematics
hultsch.summary: Edited Heronis Alexandrini Geometricorum et Stereometricorum Reliquiae (Berlin: Weidmann, 1864), establishing the first critical Greek edition of the Definitiones and the Byzantine metrological compilations (Geometrica, Stereometrica, Geodaesia) before the rediscovery of the authentic Metrica.

schmidt.name: Wilhelm Schmidt
schmidt.role: Classical philologist; editor of Teubner Hero Vols. I–II
schmidt.summary: Edited Vols. I and II.1 of the Teubner Opera omnia of Hero of Alexandria (Pneumatica, Automata, Mechanica, and Catoptrica, 1899–1900), decisively restoring the Catoptrica (De speculis) from pseudo-Ptolemy to Hero.

schoene.name: Hermann Schöne
schoene.role: Classical philologist; editio princeps editor of Hero's Metrica (1903)
schoene.summary: Following Richard Schöne's and Paul Tannery's identification of the unique 11th-century Constantinople manuscript (Codex Constantinopolitanus Palatii Veteris 1) in 1896, Hermann Schöne published the landmark 1903 Teubner editio princeps of Hero's Metrica and critical text of the Dioptra.

heiberg.name: Johan Ludvig Heiberg
heiberg.role: Danish philologist; editor of Euclid, Archimedes, Apollonius, Ptolemy, and Hero Vols. IV–V
heiberg.summary: Edited Teubner Hero Vols. IV–V (Definitiones, Geometrica, Stereometrica, 1912–1914) and discovered the Archimedes Palimpsest in Constantinople in 1906, confirming every quotation from Archimedes' Method (Ἐφοδικόν) preserved in Hero's Metrica I–II.
heiberg.hero_loci: Definitiones (Teubner Vol. IV, 1912); Metrica citations of Archimedes' Method

heath.name: Sir Thomas Little Heath
heath.role: Historian and translator of Greek mathematics
heath.summary: Synthesized Hero's mathematical corpus across The Thirteen Books of Euclid's Elements (1908, preserved in geometor/euclid) and A History of Greek Mathematics Vol. II (1921, pp. 298–354).
heath.hero_loci: geometor/euclid Heath commentary; History of Greek Mathematics II.298–354

wildberger.name: Norman J. Wildberger
wildberger.role: Mathematician; founder of Rational Trigonometry (Divine Proportions)
wildberger.summary: Formulates Archimedes' Function / Quadrea A = 16Δ² = (Q₁ + Q₂ + Q₃)² − 2(Q₁² + Q₂² + Q₃²) and rational spread/quadrance laws over arbitrary fields without square roots or transcendental functions, directly illuminating the algebraic core of Hero's Metrica I.8.

aristotle.name: Aristotle of Stagira
aristotle.summary: Formulates proportional distributive justice in Nicomachean Ethics V.3 (echoed in Hero's Metrica III Prooemium) and the teleological principle 'nature does nothing in vain' invoked in Olympiodorus's Commentary on Meteorology III.2 preserving Hero's Catoptrica shortest-path proof.
aristotle.hero_loci: Metrica III Preface; Catoptrica Greek Fragment

eupalinus.name: Eupalinus of Megara
eupalinus.role: Greek hydraulic engineer; builder of the Tunnel of Samos
eupalinus.summary: Excavated the 1,036-meter two-portal aqueduct tunnel through Mount Kastro on Samos from both hillsides simultaneously; Hero's Dioptra Ch. 15 preserves the classical Hellenistic geometric solution to the two-portal mountain-tunneling problem.

schoene-richard.name: Richard Schöne
schoene-richard.role: Classical archaeologist and philologist; discoverer of the Constantinople Metrica codex
schoene-richard.summary: Identified the lost Metrica of Hero of Alexandria in 1896 inside Codex Constantinopolitanus Palatii Veteris 1 in Constantinople and entrusted its editio princeps to his son Hermann Schöne.

neugebauer.name: Otto Neugebauer
neugebauer.role: Mathematician and historian of ancient exact sciences
neugebauer.summary: Established the definitive chronological anchor for Hero of Alexandria in 1938 by proving that the lunar eclipse observed simultaneously at Alexandria and Rome in Dioptra Ch. 35 occurred on 13 March 62 CE, and traced the Babylonian root-extraction background of Metrica I.8.
neugebauer.hero_loci: Dioptra Ch. 35 eclipse dating (62 CE); Metrica I.8
